## Ben Johnson: the designer

**Ben Johnson** is an unlikely NFL play-caller in the best sense. He was a walk-on quarterback at North Carolina
who graduated with degrees in mathematics and computer science and worked briefly as a software developer before
going into coaching: graduate assistant and then tight ends coach at Boston College, seven seasons on the Miami
Dolphins' offensive staff (quarterbacks, tight ends and receivers), and then Detroit in 2019 as an offensive
quality-control coach, the job of breaking down film and data for the coaches above him.[^johnson] Campbell's
arrival in 2021 kept him and made him passing-game coordinator. When the offense sputtered under coordinator
Anthony Lynn, Campbell took over the play-calling at midseason, leaning on Johnson for the plan; after the season
Lynn left and Johnson became the
[offensive coordinator](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offensive-coordinator) and
[play-caller](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-caller).[^lynn]

The results came fast. Detroit's offense ranked `{python} S["det_epa_rk2021"]` in EPA per play in 2021,
`{python} S["det_epa_rk2022"]` in 2022, `{python} S["det_epa_rk2023"]` in 2023 and `{python} S["det_epa_rk2024"]`
in 2024, when the Lions went `{python} S["rec_DET_2024"]` and led the league with `{python} S["det_pts24"]` points.
Goff, the castoff, threw for `{python} S["goff24_yds"]` yards and `{python} S["goff24_td"]` touchdowns that year.
Johnson was named the AP's Assistant Coach of the Year for 2024.[^acoy]

What was his offense? Not one invention. Its base was familiar: a wide-zone and gap run game, play-action off
it, and quick, timed throws to St. Brown and LaPorta. What made it *Johnson's* was a set of habits layered on top
that made every snap look like several others. Here are the four that show up most clearly on film and in the
data, with what each buys and costs.

### Habit 1: the quarterback goes back under center

In the 2010s the shotgun took over the NFL. By 2023 barely more than a quarter of snaps came with the quarterback
[under center](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center). Johnson's Lions went the other way: under center
on `{python} S["uc_DET_2022"]` of their runs and passes in 2022 (`{python} S["uc_DET_2022_rk"]` in the league;
the league average was `{python} S["uc_lg_2022"]`) and `{python} S["uc_DET_2024"]` in 2024, again the highest
rate in football (league `{python} S["uc_lg_2024"]`).[^ftn]

Why go back? Because under center, a run and a pass begin with the same motion. The quarterback turns his back to
the defense, the running back comes downhill toward him, and for the first second the linebackers can't see the
ball. From the shotgun, the run fake is a sideways mesh the defense reads more easily. Under center is a disguise
before it is anything else, and the payoff is
[**play-action**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action). In 2024 the Lions used a run fake on
`{python} S["pa_DET_2024"]` of their dropbacks, the league's highest share (league
`{python} S["pa_lg_2024"]`), and across 2022–2024 their dropbacks averaged `{python} S["det_pa_epa"]` EPA with a
run fake against `{python} S["det_nopa_epa"]` without one.

Here is the honest part. Detroit's plays from under center were not, on average, better than its plays from the
shotgun: `{python} S["det_uc_epa"]` EPA per play against `{python} S["det_gun_epa"]` in 2022–2024. That is the
point. Under center didn't win by itself; it made the run and the pass look alike, so that both worked. The cost
is in the passing game's other half: from under center the quarterback needs a beat longer to set up on a true
dropback, which is part of why under-center teams lean on play-action rather than pure drop-back passing.

### Habit 2: bodies, and the lineman who might be a receiver

Johnson loved [heavy personnel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-heavy-personnel) (extra tight ends) and
[jumbo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jumbo-six-offensive-linemen) sets with a sixth offensive lineman, and he
made that sixth lineman a weapon by having him report eligible. [Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)
counted the numbers: Detroit reported a lineman on 170 runs and passes from 2022 to 2024, third most in the
league, and passed on about 35% of them against about 24% for the league.

A reported lineman sends the defense two messages at once. "Big formation" says run, so linebackers and a safety
creep toward the line. "Eligible" says this 300-pounder might go out for a pass, so somebody has to account for
him. @fig-jumbo shows the two plays that make the defense pay for each message.

```{python}
#| label: fig-jumbo
#| fig-cap: "One jumbo look, two answers (illustrative). Six offensive linemen; #70 has reported eligible and lines up as the right end, where a tight end would stand, and the defense has walked its strong safety (SS) down to make eight in the box against the run. Left, the leak: the run fake goes left, the linebackers flow with it, #70 blocks for a count and then slips into the flat behind them while the quarterback boots right. Right, the bait: the run fake goes right, toward #70, and the safety and linebackers attack it. Z runs a deep crossing route into the space they left, while X's post holds the deep safety in the middle. Both plays start from exactly the same picture; the defense has to guess which message to believe."
def jumbo_look():
    off = line5() + [O("T70", "OL", -0.7, 4.8, "70"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
                     O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 9.5, "Z"),
                     O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("SAM", "SAM", 3.8, 7.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.4, 1.2, "M"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, -2.8, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, 4.2, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, -0.5, "FS"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -12.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.5, "CB")]
    return off, dfn


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 4.3))
LAT, WIN = (-15.5, 15.5), (-9.5, 25.0)

# --- left: the leak ---
off, dfn = jumbo_look()
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=5)
go(p, "RB", [(-4.6, -2.0), (-1.4, -3.8)], "run", speed=6.0)                  # the fake, left
go(p, "QB", [(-2.7, -1.2), (-5.2, 2.4), (-5.0, 6.8)], speed=5.0)             # fake, then boot right
go(p, "T70", [(0.2, 5.4)], "block", speed=2.0)                               # a count of blocking ...
go(p, "T70", [(2.2, 8.4), (3.0, 12.8)], "route", speed=5.0, delay=0.3)       # ... then the leak
go(p, "Z", [(9.0, 9.8), (17.0, 13.0)], "route")                              # clear out the corner
for k, to in [("MIKE", (2.6, -1.8)), ("WILL", (2.8, -5.0)), ("SAM", (3.0, 4.4)), ("SS", (4.2, 1.8))]:
    go(p, k, [to], speed=4.0)                                                # chase the fake
go(p, "RCB", [(15.0, 12.4)], speed=5.0)                                      # carries Z deep
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    go(p, k, [(-0.2, p.players[k].w - 0.7)], "block", speed=1.5)
p.pass_to("T70", t=2.6)
p.highlight("T70")
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
no_numbers(axes[0])
P = P_of(fld, p)
say(axes[0], P, -4.3, 12.2, "70: block a count,\nthen leak", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(axes[0], P, 6.0, -6.4, "linebackers chase\nthe run fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(axes[0], P, -7.4, 7.6, "Q: fake left,\nboot right", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
axes[0].set_title("The leak: throw to the lineman", fontsize=9, loc="left")

# --- right: the bait ---
off, dfn = jumbo_look()
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=5)
go(p, "RB", [(-4.4, 2.0), (-1.4, 3.8)], "run", speed=6.0)                    # the fake, right
go(p, "QB", [(-2.7, 1.0), (-6.6, -0.6)], speed=4.0)                         # fake, then set up
go(p, "Z", [(11.0, 9.0), (15.5, 1.0), (16.0, -5.0)], "route")                # deep crosser behind the bite
go(p, "X", [(12.0, -12.0), (23.0, -4.5)], "route")                           # post: hold the deep safety
for k, to in [("MIKE", (2.2, 2.6)), ("WILL", (2.6, 0.4)), ("SAM", (2.4, 5.8)), ("SS", (3.4, 4.6))]:
    go(p, k, [to], speed=4.0)                                                # attack the run fake
go(p, "FS", [(17.5, -2.6)], speed=3.0)
go(p, "RCB", [(16.0, 11.0)], speed=5.0)
go(p, "LCB", [(17.0, -10.5)], speed=5.0)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "T70"):
    go(p, k, [(0.0, p.players[k].w + 0.6)], "block", speed=1.5)
p.pass_to("Z", t=2.7)
p.highlight("Z")
fld = p.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
no_numbers(axes[1])
P = P_of(fld, p)
say(axes[1], P, 9.4, 2.4, "SS and linebackers\nattack the run fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(axes[1], P, 19.8, 7.4, "Z: deep crosser into\nthe space they left", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(axes[1], P, 21.8, -10.6, "X's post holds\nthe deep safety", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("The bait: throw behind the run defense", fontsize=9, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The left play is the one fans remember, because the catch is funny. The right one is the one that does damage,
and it is far more common. That trade is the whole design: the reported lineman is mostly a *threat*, and the
offense cashes the threat by throwing somewhere else.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Reporting a tackle eligible is a trick play." Mostly it isn't. Across the league, a reported lineman usually
means a run, and Detroit ran on about two of every three such snaps. The report is a cheap way to add a
blocker who is also a possible receiver, and the passes it sets up usually go to the regular receivers. The
genuinely tricky part, a throw to the lineman himself, is the rare constraint play that keeps the threat honest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Lions at Cowboys, December 30, 2023"}
Back to the opening play, now with the vocabulary. Trailing 20–19 with 23 seconds left, Campbell went for two
and the win on the road, the choice the [two-point chart](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)
calls close. Johnson's call put a sixth lineman on the field and threw to a tackle, and the official play-by-play
tells the story in one line: "70-D.Skipper reported in as eligible... 16-J.Goff pass to 68-T.Decker is complete. ATTEMPT
SUCCEEDS. PENALTY on DET-68-T.Decker, Illegal Touch Pass." Backup tackle Dan Skipper (#70) and Decker (#68) had
both gone toward referee Brad Allen; Decker said afterwards that he reported, Skipper said he hadn't said a word,
and Allen said that number 70 had reported. The retry moved back five yards and failed, and so did one more after
a Dallas penalty. Detroit lost 20–19.

The same game shows the rest of the identity. Earlier, on fourth-and-2 from their own 28, the Lions ran a fake
punt: a direct snap to linebacker Jalen Reeves-Maybin, who threw 31 yards to Khalil
Dorsey. When the two teams met again in October 2024, in a 47–9 Detroit win, the Lions ran a hook-and-lateral that
ended with Penei Sewell carrying the ball to the Dallas 3, called back for an ineligible man downfield, and
widely read as a joke at the expense of the 2023 game.[^troll]

**What to notice:** the play was a good idea that died on a procedure, which is a risk every reporting play
carries: the referee has to hear the report and announce it, and the defense has to be told. The lesson Detroit took was not to
stop reporting linemen; they kept doing it for two more seasons. The lesson for a viewer is to listen for the
referee's announcement, and then watch the safeties rather than the lineman.
:::

### Habit 3: shift, set, motion: make the defense declare twice

Before a defense can stop a play, it has to agree on what it's looking at: which side is the strength, which
linebacker has which gap, who covers whom. Every [shift](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shift) asks it to agree
again. Johnson's offense layered two kinds of movement: first a shift that changed the formation (a tight end
trading sides, a receiver tightening his split), then, after the required one-second freeze, a man in
[motion at the snap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion-at-the-snap). @fig-shift-motion runs one such
sequence in simulation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shift-motion
#| fig-cap: "Shift, set, motion (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking format; illustrative, not a specific Lions play). 1: two tight ends, one on each side; the defense sets its strength toward Y. 2: the shift: U walks across behind the quarterback to a wing beside Y, and Z tightens his split, so the formation is now heavy to the right. 3: the defense has to re-declare: the Sam slides out over U, the Mike and Will shuffle right, the right corner moves in over Z. Everyone on offense is set for a full second, as the rules require. 4: Z comes back across in jet motion; the left safety spins down toward him and the right safety rotates to the middle, so two-high becomes one-high, and the linebackers bump left. 5: at the snap the quarterback fakes the jet sweep to Z, and the left side of the defense reacts to it. 6: the ball goes the other way: a handoff to R on a run to the heavy right side, behind U and Y, where the defense has one fewer player than it had at the start. Dashed outlines are where players began."
def shift_play():
    off = line5() + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("U", "TE", -1.6, -6.2, "U"),
                     O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 3.8, 6.4, "S"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.0, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    # pre-snap paths (for positions); their timing is set by retime() below
    pre(p, "U", [(-3.3, -3.0), (-3.3, 3.5), (-1.6, 6.4)])
    pre(p, "Z", [(-1.5, 9.0), (-3.0, 4.0), (-3.0, 0.2)])
    for k, to in [("SAM", (3.6, 8.2)), ("RCB", (6.5, 9.8))]:
        pre(p, k, [to])
    pre(p, "MIKE", [(4.5, 2.2), (4.5, 0.9)])
    pre(p, "WILL", [(4.5, -1.6), (4.5, -3.0)])
    pre(p, "FS", [(8.0, -8.4)])
    pre(p, "SS", [(12.6, 2.5)])
    # after the snap
    go(p, "Z", [(-2.8, -8.0), (0.5, -13.5)], speed=8.0)                     # the fake jet sweep
    go(p, "QB", [(-2.4, -0.6), (-4.2, 1.4)], speed=6.0)                      # fake to Z, hand to R
    go(p, "QB", [(-6.2, -2.4)], speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
    go(p, "RB", [(-4.6, 1.8), (-1.6, 3.7), (2.4, 4.3), (9.5, 4.6)], "run", speed=6.4, delay=0.3)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.8)
    for k, dw in [("LT", -0.6), ("LG", 0.6), ("C", 0.7), ("RG", 0.7), ("RT", 0.6)]:
        go(p, k, [(0.3, p.players[k].w + dw)], "block", speed=1.5)
    go(p, "Y", [(0.4, 5.5)], "block", speed=1.6)
    go(p, "U", [(2.9, 7.7)], "block", speed=2.6)
    go(p, "X", [(3.4, -13.6)], "block", speed=4.0)
    go(p, "WILL", [(3.6, -4.8)], speed=3.5)                                  # first steps: chase the jet
    go(p, "MIKE", [(4.0, -0.4), (3.4, 2.8)], speed=3.5)                      # ... then back to the run, late
    go(p, "SAM", [(3.3, 8.4)], speed=2.0)
    go(p, "FS", [(5.6, -10.4)], speed=4.0)
    go(p, "LCB", [(4.8, -12.0)], speed=3.0)
    go(p, "SS", [(10.5, 3.4)], speed=3.0, delay=0.4)
    go(p, "LE", [(0.6, -3.2)], speed=1.5)
    go(p, "RE", [(1.0, 6.6)], speed=1.0)
    # the schedule: shift (-6.8 to -4.6), defense re-declares, everyone set, jet motion from -1.3
    retime(p, "U", [(-6.8, -1.6, -6.2), (-6.0, -3.3, -3.0), (-5.2, -3.3, 3.5), (-4.6, -1.6, 6.4)])
    retime(p, "Z", [(-6.8, -1.5, 13.0), (-5.6, -1.5, 13.0), (-4.6, -1.5, 9.0), (-1.3, -1.5, 9.0),
                    (-0.65, -3.0, 4.0), (0.0, -3.0, 0.2)])
    retime(p, "SAM", [(-6.8, 3.8, 6.4), (-4.4, 3.8, 6.4), (-3.4, 3.6, 8.2)])
    retime(p, "RCB", [(-6.8, 6.5, 13.0), (-4.4, 6.5, 13.0), (-3.4, 6.5, 9.8)])
    retime(p, "MIKE", [(-6.8, 4.5, 0.8), (-4.3, 4.5, 0.8), (-3.4, 4.5, 2.2), (-0.9, 4.5, 2.2), (0.0, 4.5, 0.9)])
    retime(p, "WILL", [(-6.8, 4.5, -3.2), (-4.3, 4.5, -3.2), (-3.4, 4.5, -1.6), (-0.9, 4.5, -1.6), (0.0, 4.5, -3.0)])
    retime(p, "FS", [(-6.8, 12.0, -8.0), (-1.0, 12.0, -8.0), (0.0, 8.0, -8.4)])
    retime(p, "SS", [(-6.8, 12.0, 8.0), (-1.0, 12.0, 8.0), (0.0, 12.6, 2.5)])
    p.highlight("U", "Z")
    p.highlight("FS", color=style.DEFENSE)
    return p


SHIFT = shift_play()
show_play(SHIFT, [-6.8, -4.6, -2.2, -0.5, 0.45, 2.5],
          ["1. Lined up: Y right, U on the left wing", "2. The shift: U trades sides, Z tightens",
           "3. Defense re-declares; all set 1 second", "4. Jet motion: FS spins down, SS to the middle",
           "5. Snap: fake the jet to Z", "6. Handoff to R, back to the heavy side"],
          phases([(-4.7, "The shift: U trades sides, Z tightens his split"),
                  (-1.3, "The defense re-declares; everyone set for a full second"),
                  (0.0, "Jet motion: the safety spins down, the linebackers bump"),
                  (0.75, "Snap: fake the jet sweep"), (9, "Hand off back to the heavy side")]),
          lateral=(-16.5, 15.5), window=(-9, 14), ghosts=("U", "Z", "SAM", "MIKE", "WILL", "FS", "SS", "RCB"),
          ghost_t=-6.8)
```

Count what the defense had to do in under seven seconds: identify a two-tight-end formation and set its strength;
watch two players move at once, re-identify the strength and slide three players; recognise a jet motion and
rotate its safeties; and then, at the snap, decide whether the jet was real. Each of those is a call that must be
heard by eleven people in a loud stadium. Each is a chance for one of them to be a step late or in the wrong
gap. A defense that answers every movement correctly has still been made to *show* its answers, which tells the
quarterback who is likely to be where.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Shifts and motion buy information and mistakes. The defense's adjustment reveals its coverage (a defender who
travels with motion suggests man; a safety who spins suggests a rotation), and every re-declaration is a chance
for a miscommunication. Layering a shift *and* a motion means the defense has to answer twice on one snap. The
cost: the offense must be perfectly drilled too. After a shift every player has to be still for a full second
before anyone goes in motion, or it is a five-yard illegal shift, and the more players move, the
more ways there are to get it wrong. It also burns play clock, which is why these sequences cluster on plays
where the offense broke the huddle early.
:::

Johnson's Lions were not the league's heaviest motion team by volume: FTN's charters logged motion on
`{python} S["mo_DET_2024"]` of Detroit's plays in 2024, `{python} S["mo_DET_2024_rk"]` in the league (the Rams led,
at `{python} S["mo_top24"]`). The distinctive thing was the combination: motion *plus* shifts *plus* under center *plus* heavy
personnel, so the same eleven players could arrive at many different formations, and the defense could rarely
substitute its way out of a look before the snap.

### Habit 4: trick plays as constraint plays

Every team has a few trick plays. Johnson's Lions ran them more than anyone and treated them as part of the
system rather than a surprise package. FTN's charters flagged `{python} S["det_trick_n"]` Detroit snaps as trick
plays from 2022 to 2025, the most in the league (the next team had `{python} S["trick_n2"]`), and those snaps
averaged `{python} S["det_trick_epa"]` EPA, against `{python} S["lg_trick_epa"]` for everyone's trick plays.[^ftn2]
The samples are small, a few dozen plays, so read the EPA as "worked often" rather than as a precise number.

The logic is [constraint theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd). A trick
play isn't random. It is a [constraint play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-constraint-play) built on a specific
habit the defense has learned from your film: a cornerback who always rallies to a short catch, a defense that
ignores the running back as a passer, a safety who flies at every run fake. The offense's own
[self-scout](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-self-scout) tells it which of its plays the defense has studied
hardest, and the trick play starts as exactly that play. The 2024 season shows the pattern: the same catch-and-pitch
idea four times, and three different non-quarterbacks throwing.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tricks
#| tbl-cap: "The 2024 Lions' trick plays, from the official play-by-play (regular season and playoffs). Result yards include the lateral; EPA is the play's expected points added. Source: nflverse play-by-play; dates from nflverse schedules."
TRICKS = [
    ("2024_03_DET_ARI", "Lateral to 26-J.Gibbs", "Hook-and-lateral: St. Brown catches, pitches to Gibbs"),
    ("2024_04_SEA_DET", "pass short left to 16-J.Goff", "St. Brown throws to Goff"),
    ("2024_06_DET_DAL", "Lateral to 58-P.Sewell", "Hook-and-lateral to right tackle Sewell"),
    ("2024_08_TEN_DET", "D.Montgomery pass", "Running back Montgomery throws to LaPorta"),
    ("2024_13_CHI_DET", "P.Sewell sacked", "Toss to Sewell, with an option to pass"),
    ("2024_15_BUF_DET", "Lateral to 26-J.Gibbs", "Hook-and-lateral: St. Brown to Gibbs"),
    ("2024_17_DET_SF", "Lateral to 9-Ja.Williams", "Hook-and-lateral: St. Brown to Jameson Williams"),
    ("2024_20_WAS_DET", "D.Montgomery pass", "Montgomery throws to St. Brown"),
    ("2024_20_WAS_DET", "Ja.Williams pass", "Jameson Williams throws to Gibbs"),
]
allsch = nfl().load_schedules([2024]).to_pandas().set_index("game_id")
r24 = raw[raw.season == 2024]
md = ("| Date | Opp. | Down | Play | Result | EPA |\n"
      "|-----------|--------|--------|------------------------------------|-------------|-----:|\n")
for gid, key, what in TRICKS:
    row = r24[(r24.game_id == gid) & r24.desc.str.contains(key, regex=False, na=False)].iloc[0]
    g = allsch.loc[gid]
    opp = g.away_team if g.home_team == "DET" else g.home_team
    when = pd.Timestamp(g.gameday).strftime("%b %-d, %Y") + (" (playoff)" if g.game_type != "REG" else "")
    dd = f"{['1st', '2nd', '3rd', '4th'][int(row.down) - 1]}-{int(row.ydstogo)}"
    if "No Play" in row.desc:
        res = "no play (penalty)"
    elif "INTERCEPTED" in row.desc:
        res = "intercepted"
    elif "TOUCHDOWN" in row.desc:
        res = f"{int(row.yards_gained)}-yard TD"
    else:
        yg = int(row.yards_gained)
        res = f"{'−' if yg < 0 else '+'}{abs(yg)} yard{'' if abs(yg) == 1 else 's'}"
    md += f"| {when} | {'at ' if g.home_team != 'DET' else ''}{opp} | {dd} | {what} | {res} | {row.epa:+.1f} |\n"
display(Markdown(md))
```

Notice two things in the table. The hook-and-lateral kept working after opponents had surely seen it on film,
because the defense's habit it attacks, swarming the receiver who has just caught a short pass, is one no coach
wants to un-teach. And the last two rows are the cost of the habit: in the season's biggest game, two trick plays,
one a 20-yard gain and one intercepted in the fourth quarter.

The most famous of them is @fig-hook-lateral: on a Monday night in Santa Clara, St. Brown caught a pass a yard
past the line of scrimmage and pitched it to Jameson Williams, who ran 41 more yards for a touchdown.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hook-lateral
#| fig-cap: "The hook-and-lateral (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking format; illustrative, not the exact alignment the Lions used). 1: at the snap Z, the outside receiver, runs a two-yard hitch toward the sideline; H, inside him, starts late on a flat path toward the sideline. 2: the quarterback throws quickly to Z, and the three nearest defenders (the corner, the nickel and the safety) all break on the catch: tackling the man with the ball is what they are trained to do. 3: as H passes just behind him, Z pitches the ball backward to H. A backward pass can be thrown to anyone, at any time, so this is legal anywhere on the field. 4: three defenders are now on the wrong man, and H has the sideline to himself. The pitch has to go backward or level, or it is an illegal forward pass."
def hook_play():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.5, -8.0, "Y"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, 8.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.5, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 8.4, "NB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.5, 15.0, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0, "CB"),
           D("SS", "SS", 11.5, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=58, to_go=12)
    go(p, "Z", [(2.3, 14.6), (1.9, 14.2)], "route", speed=7.0)
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=0.75)
    go(p, "H", [(-0.9, 10.6), (0.5, 13.0), (0.7, 15.2), (4.0, 17.5), (10.0, 19.0), (17.5, 19.8)], "route",
       speed=6.6, delay=0.85)
    p.pitch("H", t=1.95)
    go(p, "RCB", [(2.8, 14.6), (2.2, 14.1)], speed=3.6, delay=0.75)
    go(p, "NB", [(2.9, 12.3), (2.4, 13.3)], speed=5.0, delay=0.85)
    go(p, "SS", [(5.4, 13.4), (3.2, 14.0)], speed=6.0, delay=0.8)
    go(p, "MIKE", [(3.2, 8.6)], speed=4.5, delay=0.9)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        go(p, k, [(-0.8, p.players[k].w)], "block", speed=1.2)
    p.highlight("Z", "H")
    return p


HOOK = hook_play()
show_play(HOOK, [0.0, 1.65, 2.0, 2.95],
          ["1. Snap: Z hitches, H starts late", "2. The catch: three defenders break on Z",
           "3. The pitch, backward, to H", "4. H has the sideline"],
          phases([(0.7, "Z runs a short hitch; H starts late"), (1.6, "Quick throw to Z"),
                  (1.95, "Three defenders break on the catch"), (2.4, "Pitch to H, backward"),
                  (9, "H has the sideline")]),
          lateral=(-5.6, 26.6), window=(-7.5, 19.5), ghosts=("RCB", "NB", "SS"), ghost_t=0.0, trail_from=0.0)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game a trick play is a menu option you pick when you're feeling lucky. In the NFL it is a scheduled
part of the week. A trick play is usually installed against one opponent's habit, practised all week, and called
when the situation matches the film: the right down, the right hash, the right defensive call. Coaches think of
it like any other [tendency breaker](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-breaker): it exists because the
offense has been predictable on purpose, and it works only if the play it imitates has been run often enough
that the defense trusts its read.
:::

## Dan Campbell's fourth down

Johnson designed the plays; Campbell decided when to keep the offense on the field. The case for going for it on
fourth down, and the rules of thumb, are in [The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd),
along with the 2023 NFC Championship Game in San Francisco, where two fourth-down attempts failed in a 34–31 loss.
This section asks the case-study questions: how aggressive were the Lions, compared with whom, and did it pay?

```{python}
#| label: fig-fourth-down
#| fig-cap: "Left: how often each team went for it on a neutral fourth down (first three quarters, win probability 20–80%, so the decision is a choice rather than desperation), 2018–2025. The shaded band is the middle 80% of teams each season. Detroit was a below-average team on this measure before Campbell, jumped in 2021, and led the league in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Right: a rough value check, 2021–2025, first three quarters. Each dot is a team: how many times it went for it (across) against the average points gained per attempt (up), estimated as the attempt's EPA minus the league's average EPA on punts and field goals from the same distance and field position. Detroit went for it more than anyone, and on average each attempt was worth a little more than the league's, but less per attempt than teams like Philadelphia (whose tries leaned heavily on the tush push) and Kansas City. Fakes from punt formation count as attempts. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 3.4), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.12, 1]))
yrs = list(range(2018, 2026))
a.fill_between(yrs, GR.quantile(0.1, axis=1).loc[yrs], GR.quantile(0.9, axis=1).loc[yrs], color=style.GRID,
               alpha=0.9, lw=0, label="middle 80% of teams")
a.plot(yrs, LGR.loc[yrs], color=LEAGUE, lw=1.6, label="league")
a.plot(yrs, GR.loc[yrs, "DET"], color=LIONS, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3.6, label="Lions")
a.axvline(2020.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
a.text(2020.65, 0.012, "Campbell\nhired", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
a.set_ylim(0, 0.40)
a.set_xticks(yrs[::2])
a.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a.set_ylabel("Neutral fourth downs: went for it", fontsize=8)
a.set_title("Go rate", fontsize=9.5)
a.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=6.8, frameon=True, facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor="none", framealpha=1.0)

tg = TEAMGAIN.copy()
b.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
b.axhline(GOS.gain.mean(), color=LEAGUE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
b.text(tg.n.min() - 2, GOS.gain.mean() + 0.06, "league average", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
b.text(tg.n.min() - 2, -0.06, "same as kicking", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
other = tg.drop("DET")
b.scatter(other.n, other.per, s=16, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.7, lw=0)
named = tg.loc[["PHI", "KC", "CHI"]]
b.scatter(named.n, named.per, s=22, color=style.INK_2, lw=0, zorder=4)
b.scatter([tg.loc["DET", "n"]], [tg.loc["DET", "per"]], s=42, color=LIONS, zorder=5)
for t, name, dx, dy, ha in [("DET", "Lions", -3, 0.12, "right"), ("PHI", "Eagles", 3, 0.0, "left"),
                            ("KC", "Chiefs", 3, 0.0, "left"), ("CHI", "Bears", 3, -0.05, "left")]:
    b.text(tg.loc[t, "n"] + dx, tg.loc[t, "per"] + dy, name, fontsize=7, ha=ha, va="center",
           color=LIONS if t == "DET" else style.INK, fontweight="bold" if t == "DET" else "normal")
b.set_xlabel("Fourth-down attempts, 2021–2025 (first three quarters)", fontsize=7.6)
b.set_ylabel("Points gained per attempt vs kicking", fontsize=8)
b.set_title("Value per attempt", fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

Three readings of @fig-fourth-down.

**The habit came first, the good team second.** Detroit's neutral go rate was `{python} S["det_gr2020"]` in 2020,
below the league. In Campbell's first season it was `{python} S["det_gr2021"]`, `{python} S["det_gr_rk2021"]` in
the league, for a team that won three games: the underdog logic from the start of this chapter. Then it *stayed*
near a third of neutral fourth downs, first in the league in 2022, 2023 and 2024
(`{python} S["det_gr2024"]` in 2024, against a league average of `{python} S["lg_gr2024"]`), after Detroit had
become a favourite. That is the more interesting decision, because the variance argument no longer applies. A
favourite going for it is betting on the expected-points case alone, and on its own offense.

**It paid, by a rough yardstick, about two touchdowns a season.** Detroit converted `{python} S["det_conv"]` of its
attempts in 2021–2025 (the league converted `{python} S["lg_conv"]`). Converting is the wrong test, though, as
[10-04](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) argued: what matters is the attempt
compared with the kick it replaced. Compare each of Detroit's `{python} S["det_n_q3"]` first-three-quarter attempts
with what the league's punts and field goals produced from the same spots, and the attempts come out about
`{python} S["det_gain"]` points ahead over five seasons, roughly `{python} S["det_gain_yr"]` a season, with the best
year in 2024 (about `{python} S["gain24"]`). That ranks `{python} S["gain_rk"]` in the league over the period.
This yardstick is crude. Teams go for it when they like their chances, so the attempts are a selected sample, and a
proper answer needs a win-probability model of each decision, which is built in
[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd). But
the direction is not in doubt.

**The more you go, the less each go is worth.** Look at the right panel again. Detroit is far out to the right, the
league's busiest fourth-down team, but its value *per attempt* (`{python} S["det_per"]` points) is only a little
above the league's (`{python} S["lg_per"]`), and well below the Eagles (`{python} S["per_PHI"]`) and the Chiefs
(`{python} S["per_KC"]`). That's what diminishing returns look like. The first fourth downs a coach adds are the
obvious ones, fourth-and-1 near midfield. The next ones are closer calls: `{python} S["det_long"]` of Detroit's
attempts came with four or more yards to go, against `{python} S["lg_long"]` for the league. A closer call is still
worth taking if it's positive on average, but it fails more often, and its failures are the ones that end up on
highlight shows.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Campbell is a gambler." A gambler takes bets with negative expected value for the thrill. Campbell's fourth-down
record is a long series of bets with *positive* expected value, some of which lost, a few of them in playoff
games. The fair criticism is narrower: in a handful of late, high-leverage spots (the 2023 NFC title game is the
famous one), the models themselves called the decision close, and a coach with a strong kicker might reasonably
have kicked. Judge the habit by the whole record, and the close calls by the odds before the snap.
:::

The habit extended past the field. Detroit's front office took its aggressive streak to the league's rule-making
meetings: a Lions proposal produced the 2024 rule that gives a coach a third challenge when *either* of his first
two succeeds (it had required both),[^challenge] and in 2025 the Lions proposed letting wild-card teams with better
records be seeded above division winners, a proposal withdrawn before a vote.[^seeding] A team that thinks in
expected value tends to notice where the rules leave value on the table.

## How opponents responded

Defenses tried the normal things. They could not take away the under-center play-action game by playing two deep
safeties all day, because Detroit's run game would then face a light box; in 2024 Detroit saw a two-high shell on
`{python} S["two_det24"]` of its dropbacks, `{python} S["two_det24_rk"]` in the league (league
`{python} S["two_lg24"]`), meaning defenses more often brought a safety down to stop the run and accepted the
play-action risk. That's the trade Johnson's offense was built to force.

The most effective response came in January 2025, in the divisional round against Washington. Detroit, the
`{python} S["rec_DET_2024"]` top seed, lost 45–31 after turning the ball over five times: four interceptions, one
of them returned for a touchdown, and a lost fumble. Two of the trick plays in the table above came in that game.
A team built on variance had the bad tail arrive on the worst day.

The league's response was the more durable one, and it came in two forms. The first was imitation, though the
Lions were one influence among several (by 2025 the Rams took more snaps from under center than anyone): league-wide, the
share of plays from under center went from about 27% in 2023 to about 34% in 2025, heavy personnel climbed to a
decade high, and the neutral fourth-down go rate kept rising.[^trend] The second was the coaching market. Within
three days in January 2025, the Lions lost both coordinators to head-coaching jobs: Johnson to the Chicago Bears,
a division rival, and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn to the New York Jets.[^depart] That is the usual price of
success for a staff, and it set up the natural experiment in the rest of this chapter.

## After Johnson: Detroit in 2025 and 2026

Campbell hired John Morton, a veteran assistant, as offensive coordinator and play-caller, and Kelvin Sheppard
replaced Glenn as defensive coordinator. After a loss to Minnesota in Week 9, Campbell took the play sheet himself,
starting with a 44–22 win over Washington.[^morton] The Lions finished `{python} S["rec_DET_2025"]` and missed the
playoffs. The offense was still good, `{python} S["det_epa_rk2025"]` in EPA per play, with the same quarterback,
receivers and running backs, but no longer great, and it looked more like everyone else's: under center
`{python} S["uc_DET_2025"]` of the time (from `{python} S["uc_DET_2024"]`), play-action on `{python} S["pa_DET_2025"]`
of dropbacks (from `{python} S["pa_DET_2024"]`). [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
compares the offense under Morton and under Campbell in detail. After the season Morton was fired, and the Lions
hired Drew Petzing, previously the Cardinals' coordinator, as their third offensive coordinator in three years;
Sheppard stayed on defense.[^petzing]

## What transferred to Chicago

The Bears Johnson inherited were a classic Detroit-2021 problem: `{python} S["rec_CHI_2024"]` in 2024, an offense
`{python} S["chi_epa_rk2024"]` in EPA per play, and a rookie quarterback, Caleb Williams, sacked
`{python} S["chi_sk24"]` times. In 2025 they went `{python} S["rec_CHI_2025"]`, won the NFC North, beat Green Bay
31–27 in the wild-card round (the franchise's first playoff win since the 2010 season) and lost to the Rams 20–17 in overtime in the divisional round.[^bears25] The offense
jumped to `{python} S["chi_epa_rk2025"]` in EPA per play; Williams was sacked `{python} S["chi_sk25"]` times, and his
EPA per dropback rose from `{python} S["cw24_epa"]` to `{python} S["cw25_epa"]`.

How much of that is Johnson? @fig-transfer compares the two teams' fingerprints before and after he moved.

```{python}
#| label: fig-transfer
#| fig-cap: "What moved with Ben Johnson. Each arrow runs from a team's 2024 value to its 2025 value; the grey tick is the 2025 league average. Johnson's habits (under center, play-action and trick plays) jumped in Chicago in his first season and fell back toward the league in Detroit without him. The fourth-down habit belonged to the other coach: Detroit stayed more aggressive than the league under Campbell, while Chicago's go rate rose about as much as the league's did. Trick plays are FTN's flag per 100 runs and passes; play-action is a share of dropbacks; under center and trick plays are shares of runs and passes; the go rate uses neutral fourth downs as in the previous figure. Sources: FTN charting via nflverse; nflverse play-by-play."
METRICS = [("Under center (% of plays)", HAB["uc"] * 100, HABL["uc"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Play-action (% of dropbacks)", HAB["pa"] * 100, HABL["pa"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Trick plays (per 100 plays)", HAB["tr"], HABL["tr"], "{:.1f}"),
           ("Neutral 4th-down go rate (%)", GR.loc[2022:] * 100, LGR.loc[2022:] * 100, "{:.0f}%")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, (title, tab, lg, fmt) in zip(axes.flat, METRICS):
    vals = [tab.loc[[2024, 2025], t].values for t in ("DET", "CHI")]
    hi = max(max(v) for v in vals + [[lg.loc[2025]]])
    for i, (team, col, v) in enumerate([("Lions", LIONS, vals[0]), ("Bears", BEARS, vals[1])]):
        y = 1 - i
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((v[0], y), (v[1], y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=col, lw=2.0,
                                     shrinkA=3, shrinkB=1))
        ax.plot([v[0]], [y], marker="o", ms=4, color=col, mfc="white", mew=1.4)
        lo_, hi_ = sorted(v)
        ax.text(v[0] + (-0.025 if v[0] < v[1] else 0.025) * hi * 1.25, y + 0.3, fmt.format(v[0]), fontsize=6.6,
                ha="right" if v[0] < v[1] else "left", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
        ax.text(v[1] + (0.025 if v[0] < v[1] else -0.025) * hi * 1.25, y + 0.3, fmt.format(v[1]), fontsize=6.6,
                ha="left" if v[0] < v[1] else "right", va="center", color=col, fontweight="bold")
    ax.axvline(lg.loc[2025], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.2, ymin=0.05, ymax=0.95)
    ax.set_yticks([1, 0], ["Lions", "Bears"], fontsize=7.6)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.75)
    ax.set_xlim(0, hi * 1.3)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.4)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=style.INK_2, marker="o", mfc="white", lw=1.6, label="2024 → 2025"),
                    Line2D([], [], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.2, label="league average, 2025")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=1.4, rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

The picture is unusually clean for football data. In one offseason, Chicago went from `{python} S["uc_CHI_2024_rk"]`
to `{python} S["uc_CHI_2025_rk"]` in under-center rate (`{python} S["uc_CHI_2024"]` to `{python} S["uc_CHI_2025"]`),
from `{python} S["pa_CHI_2024_rk"]` to `{python} S["pa_CHI_2025_rk"]` in play-action share (`{python} S["pa_CHI_2024"]`
to `{python} S["pa_CHI_2025"]`), and from `{python} S["tr_CHI_2024_rk"]` to `{python} S["tr_CHI_2025_rk"]` in
trick-play rate. Detroit's numbers moved the other way. The habits were the play-caller's, and they travelled with
him.

The fourth-down habit didn't travel the same way. Detroit's neutral go rate fell from `{python} S["det_gr2024"]` to
`{python} S["det_gr2025"]` but stayed `{python} S["det_gr_rk2025"]` in the league under Campbell; Chicago's rose from
`{python} S["chi_gr24"]` to `{python} S["chi_gr25"]`, in a season when the whole league rose. Aggression on fourth
down had been the head coach's.

What the fingerprint can't tell you is how much of Chicago's improvement came from the scheme. The Bears also rebuilt
the middle of their offensive line before 2025, trading for guards Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson (a Lions starter in
Johnson's first two seasons as coordinator) and signing center Drew Dalman,[^bearsol] and Williams was in his second
season, when most young quarterbacks improve. The sack total falling from `{python} S["chi_sk24"]` to
`{python} S["chi_sk25"]` belongs to all three. An honest summary: the *style* transferred completely and at once; the
*results* transferred substantially, with help.

## What survives

The Johnson-Campbell Lions lasted four seasons as a unit, from 2021 to 2024, and they leave a few ideas that have
outlasted the staff.

- **Under center is a disguise, not a throwback.** The Lions, with the Rams, showed that a modern passing
  offense can take a large share of its snaps from under center and gain from it, because the run fake and the run
  look the same. The league followed.
- **Personnel is a message you can lie with.** A reported lineman, a third tight end, a jumbo set: each tells the
  defense something, and an offense can choose whether to deliver on it.
- **Make the defense answer twice.** Shifts layered with motion turn a single snap into two or three communication
  tests. Most defenses pass most of them; the offense only needs the occasional failure.
- **Trick plays are part of the system.** Built on the defense's habits and the offense's own self-scout, they are
  constraint plays with a sense of humour, and their cost is visible on the bad days.
- **Fourth-down aggression became normal, and its edge got smaller.** When one team goes for it a third of the time,
  it's a strategy; when the league catches up, the remaining edge is in choosing *which* fourth downs, which is a
  harder skill to see from the stands.
- **A rebuild can choose variance.** A bad team that plays to the expected-value math and accepts the ugly
  failures can turn into a good team that keeps doing it, which is what Detroit did.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the trick detector"}
Pick a Lions or Bears game (or any team that runs a lot from under center) and flag every snap with something
unusual in it.

- **Before the snap, listen.** "Number 70 is reporting as eligible": note the down and distance. Then watch the
  safeties, not the lineman. If they creep down, expect the run fake and a throw behind them.
- **Count the movements.** One mark for a shift, one for a motion. Snaps with two or more marks are the ones where
  the defense has to communicate twice; look for a defender still pointing or moving at the snap.
- **Find the odd alignment.** A quarterback split wide, a running back alone in the backfield taking a direct snap,
  a receiver stacked right behind another one a yard off the line, a tackle at the end of the line. Write down
  what the defense did about it.
- **After the snap: who caught the first ball?** On a short catch near the sideline, keep your eyes on the player
  *behind* the catcher. If someone is trailing at full speed, the hook-and-lateral is on.
- **On fourth down, guess first.** Before the offense decides, say go, kick or punt using the rules of thumb from
  10-04. Then compare with what the coach did, and note whether he was more or less aggressive than you.
- **At the end of the game,** count your flags and how many of them gained yards. You have just charted a team's
  disguise rate, the raw material for a [tendency report](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-report).
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** Second-and-5 at your own 35, first quarter. The offense comes out in @fig-predict-1: six offensive
linemen, number 70 has reported eligible and stands at the right end of the line, the quarterback is under center
and the defense has walked a safety down, with only one deep safety left. You have seen this offense run from this
look three times already today. What is the most likely play, and where is the ball going?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: jumbo with a reported tackle (#70), second-and-5. The strong safety (ringed) has come down to about six yards deep, just outside #70, making eight defenders in the box; one deep safety remains."
off, dfn = jumbo_look()
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.2, w=5.6) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=5, title="Drill 1: number 70 has reported eligible")
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.highlight("T70")
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-9.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (10.2, 9.8), (6.2, 5.6), "safety walked down:\neight in the box")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.6, 8.4), (-0.7, 4.8), "#70 reported eligible")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (15.0, 7.4), (13.5, -0.5), "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A play-action pass behind the safety, most likely to a receiver crossing into the space he left.** Everything
in the picture says run: second-and-short, six linemen, a quarterback under center, and you've seen runs from it.
The defense agrees, which is why the safety is down. That is the bait half of @fig-jumbo. With eight defenders
committed to the run and one deep safety in the middle, the space behind the linebackers and outside the deep
safety is open for a moment after the run fake. The throw to #70 himself (the leak) is the backup, likely only if
the linebackers flow hard *away* from his side. A plain run is still possible, but the offense has spent three
snaps teaching this defense to bring the safety down. Detroit cashed exactly this kind of setup in Week 18 of 2023:
on second-and-5 with Dan Skipper reported eligible, Goff faked the run and hit St. Brown for a 70-yard touchdown
(the play is in [Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Fourth-and-2 at the opponent's 37, second quarter, score tied. @fig-predict-2 shows the field. Your
kicker makes about two-thirds of his kicks from 50 to 54 yards. What would the 2022–2024 Lions have done, what
do the rules of thumb say, and if they go for it, what kind of play would you expect from this offense?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: fourth-and-2 at the opponent's 37 (offense moving left to right). A field goal from here is about a 55-yard kick: 37 yards to the goal line, 10 more to the goalposts at the back of the end zone, and about 8 for the snap and hold. A punt would net perhaps 25 to 30 yards."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.6))
LOS, Y0 = 110 - 37, 26.65
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=LOS, window=(-22, 48), to_go=2, numbers=False, hashes=True,
            lateral=(13.0, 40.3))
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((LOS, Y0), 1.6, 1.0, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))
for x, lab in [(60, "50"), (70, "40"), (80, "30"), (90, "20"), (100, "10"), (110, "G")]:
    ax.text(x, 15.0, lab, fontsize=8, ha="center", va="center", color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold")
ax.annotate("", xy=(120, 35.2), xytext=(LOS - 8, 35.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
ax.text((LOS - 8 + 120) / 2, 37.6, "field goal: about a 55-yard kick (holder ~8 yards back; posts at the end line)",
        fontsize=7.0, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(LOS + 2, 21.0), xytext=(LOS, 21.0),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4))
ax.text(LOS + 3.0, 21.0, "2 yards for a first down", fontsize=7.2, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(LOS - 1.6, 28.6, "fourth-and-2,\nball on the\nopponent's 37", fontsize=7.0, ha="right", va="center",
        color=style.INK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(115, 24.0, "end\nzone", fontsize=7.4, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go for it, and expect a run or a quick play-action throw from under center.** This is the "go zone" from
[10-04](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd): the opponent's 30 to 40, too far for a
comfortable field goal (a 55-yarder at two-thirds or less) and too close for a punt to gain much. On fourth-and-2
teams convert a bit more than half the time, and success keeps a drive alive in field-goal range. The 2022–2024
Lions went for it on about a third of *all* neutral fourth downs, and on fourth-and-1 or 2 between the opponent's
30 and 40 in the first three quarters they went for it `{python} S["det_d2"]` of the time, a small sample of
`{python} S["det_d2_n"]` snaps (the league: `{python} S["lg_d2"]`). As for the play: Detroit's short-yardage menu was the same as its base offense, a heavy formation under
center that threatens a downhill run and the play-action pass off it. Because the defense knows a go is likely, the
first answer is often the play that looks like the run and isn't. In the 2023 NFC Championship Game, Detroit's
fourth-and-2 from the 49ers' 28 was a pass, and it fell incomplete: same reasoning, bad result.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** Second-and-goal from the 3. The offense lines up in @fig-predict-3: the running back is alone in the
shotgun spot, the quarterback is split out in the left slot, and there are two tight ends to the right, one on the
line and one on the wing, with a receiver outside them. What is the default play, what is the trick, and whom should the defense not forget?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: a direct snap to the running back (R) at the 3-yard line, with the quarterback (Q, ringed) split out in the left slot and two tight ends (Y on the line, U on the wing) to the right. Illustrative alignment."
off = line5() + [O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 0.0, "R"), O("QB", "QB", -1.5, -8.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -13.0, "X"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -1.6, 6.4, "U"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 12.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 0.9, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 0.9, -1.0, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 0.9, 1.0, "T"),
       D("RE", "DE", 0.9, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.0, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.0, 1.2, "M"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 2.6, 7.6, "S"), D("NB", "NB", 2.6, -8.4, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -13.0, "CB"),
       D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 12.5, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=107, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: a direct snap at the 3")
p.highlight("QB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-8.5, 13.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.4, -11.5), (-1.5, -8.0), "the quarterback,\nsplit out")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-6.4, 6.4), (-5.0, 0.0), "direct snap\nto the back")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The default is a run by the back who takes the snap, behind the wing tight end as an extra blocker; the trick is
a pass by that back, and the man not to forget is a tight end.** A direct snap at the goal line is a numbers play: the back
can run without a handoff, and the quarterback, standing in the slot as a receiver, takes a defender with him. The
defense's eyes go to the back and to the quarterback (everyone knows the quarterback can catch out there). What it
tends to forget is that the back can throw, and that the tight ends, the players who block on almost every goal-line
snap, are eligible. In Week 5 of 2025 at Cincinnati, Detroit took a direct snap to David Montgomery on
second-and-3 from the 3, and Montgomery threw a touchdown pass to tight end Brock Wright.[^cin] If the defense
covers the quarterback and the back's run, the tight end on the line is the most likely target.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Detroit's 2021 rebuild had two halves: build the lines and the core through the draft (Sewell, Hutchinson, St.
  Brown, Gibbs, LaPorta), and **choose variance** as an underdog. The fourth-down aggression came before the good team
  did.
- **Ben Johnson's offense (2022–2024)** was a familiar run and play-action base with four habits on top: the
  quarterback **under center** (the league's highest share in 2022 and 2024), **heavy and jumbo personnel with a
  reported lineman**, **shifts layered with motion**, and **trick plays built as constraint plays**. Each makes
  one snap look like several; each costs drilling time, play clock and the occasional disaster.
- **Campbell's fourth downs** led the league in neutral go rate in 2022–2024 and, by a rough yardstick, gained about
  two touchdowns a season over kicking, with less value per attempt than more selective teams: aggression has
  diminishing returns.
- Opponents mostly couldn't scheme the offense away; they **hired its coordinators**. Johnson went to the Bears and
  Glenn to the Jets in January 2025. Detroit then went through Morton, Campbell calling plays and, in 2026, Petzing:
  three coordinators in three years.
- **What transferred:** in one season Chicago's under-center, play-action and trick-play rates jumped to the top of
  the league and Detroit's fell back. The **style moved with the play-caller**, the **fourth-down habit stayed with
  the head coach**, and the Bears' results moved with help from a rebuilt line and a second-year quarterback.
